about: Hand-curated approximate flows for periods before the UN DESA stock data begin (1990). Rounded figures recalled from the cited literature; they were not re-checked line by line against the sources, so treat them as order-of-magnitude. 'in' = people moving to Poland, 'out' = people leaving Poland. Country code SUN = Soviet Union (drawn on Russia). Internal resettlement (for example Operation Vistula, 1947) is not migration to or from Poland and is excluded.

rows.method: Poles returning to Poland from Germany (forced labourers, prisoners of war, concentration-camp survivors and displaced persons), 1945-1950, as counted by the historian Krystyna Kersten; practically all returns were in 1945-48.
rows.why: Only about half is registered: the organised repatriation from the three Western zones was 793,733 (to August 1948). The rest, from the Soviet zone and from the spontaneous returns of 1945, was never registered, so Kersten's total is an estimate. I have read her total only as cited by others, and it includes 1950. It also counts Poles who had lived in Germany before the war.
rows.note: Kersten (1974) puts repatriation from Germany in 1945-50 at 1,642,500, from other European countries at 298,500 and from outside Europe at 8,000 (about 1.95 million in all, excluding people moved from the former eastern territories). Organised repatriation from the Western zones, from her Table 15: to 1 January 1946: 196,585 from the American zone, 14,933 from the French and 155,845 from the British; during 1946: 130,605, 26,517 and 200,816; January to June 1947: 26,258, 3,563 and 12,625; July 1947 to August 1948 (as printed): 10,731, 1,437 and 13,818; in all 364,179, 46,450 and 383,104 = 793,733 (plus 71,904 from Austria). About 700,000 Polish forced labourers and prisoners of war were in the Soviet zone at the end of the war. At the end of September 1945 there were still 816,012 Poles in the Western zones (Proudfoot, cited by Knapton), and Polish repatriation from there slowed to 79,932 between December 1945 and March 1946. This replaces the earlier midpoint of 1.5 to 2 million.
rows.source: Krystyna Kersten, Repatriacja ludnosci polskiej po II wojnie swiatowej (Wroclaw 1974), as cited by Konkret24, https://konkret24.tvn24.pl/polityka/wybory-2023-morawiecki-polacy-pierwszy-raz-od-200-lat-masowo-wracaja-z-emigracji-nie-ma-na-to-danych-st7364192; Urszula Kurcewicz, Acta Universitatis Lodziensis, Folia Historica 117 (2024), Table 15 after Kersten pp. 216-217, https://czasopisma.uni.lodz.pl/historica/article/download/25775/25605; Samantha K. Knapton, European History Quarterly 50(4) (2020), https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/75580/7/Published_Version.pdf

rows.method: Germans removed from the territories that became Polish: about 400,000 expelled before the Potsdam conference (mid-1945) plus 2,871,665 in the organised expulsions from the Potsdam conference to the end of 1949 (about 600,000 in the second half of 1945, 1,620,610 in 1946, about 536,000 in 1947, 49,145 in 1948 and 65,520 in 1949), total 3,271,665 (Nitschke), rounded.
rows.why: About 70% (1946-49, 2.27 million) rests on Polish interior-ministry transport statistics; the rest, the removals in 1945, is an estimate that sources put anywhere from 365,000 to 1.2 million. The West German Dokumentation der Vertreibung assumes about 400,000 for all of 1945, which would make the total about 2.7 million. The 1946 census counted only 2,288,300 Germans, and Nitschke thinks it undercounted by 15-20%.
rows.note: Organised expulsions by year (Polish Ministry of the Interior data, Nitschke): 1946: 1,620,610 (1,192,788 to the British zone, 427,822 to the Soviet zone); 1947: about 536,000 (the ministries' figures run from 534,961 to 572,529); 1948: 49,145; 1949: 65,520. Jankowiak (IPN) gives 2,189,286 Germans in 1,337 transports from the start of the action to 31 December 1947, against about 2,157,000 for 1946-47 here. Another 60,000 or so left in 1950 and about 150,000 Germans in 1950-59; those are not in this period. The Allied Control Council plan of 20 November 1945 foresaw 3.5 million, and Sienkiewicz and Hryciuk's atlas is cited at 3.092 million Germans moved from Poland in 1945-50 (Hrynicki and Widerski). German-side totals for people who arrived from all the eastern territories are higher because they include the pre-war German provinces and other countries.
rows.source: Bernadetta Nitschke, 'Wysiedlenia i wyjazdy ludnosci niemieckiej z Polski w latach 1945-1959', Studia Zachodnie 3 (1998), https://zbc.uz.zgora.pl/Content/45907/PDF/14_nitschke_wysiedlenia.pdf; Stanislaw Jankowiak, 'Wysiedlenia Niemcow z Polski po II wojnie swiatowej', Pamiec i Sprawiedliwosc 3/2 (2004), https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/texts/pamiec-i-sprawiedliwosc/2004-tom-3-numer-2-6/pamiec_i_sprawiedliwosc-r2004-t3-n2_6-s139-160.pdf; Wojciech Hrynicki and Jaroslaw Widerski, Kultura Bezpieczenstwa 24 (2016), https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/texts/kultura-bezpieczenstwa-nauka-praktyka-refleksje/2016-numer-24/kultura_bezpieczenstwa_nauka_praktyka_refleksje-r2016-t-n24-s92-117.pdf

rows.note: Arrivals in Poland from USSR territory, by year: 1945: 723,488; 1946: 644,437; 1947: 10,801 (PUR, GUS Rocznik 1948 table 6, which totals 1,495,938 for Oct 1944 to 1947 with 117,212 in 1944); 1948: 7,325 (repatriations, Bartoszewicz citing GUS Rocznik 1949). Sum 1,386,051. Excluded: 117,212 arrivals in 1944, and 22,815 more who came by road during the whole action (the table's footnote). Table 6 splits the total into resettled from the Ukrainian, Belarusian and Lithuanian SSRs (787,600 + 274,163 + 178,013) and repatriated from the rest of the USSR (256,162); Bartoszewicz gives 1,503,263 for 1944-48, which equals the table's 1,495,938 plus 7,325 and confirms it. 1949 is not included (no figure found). Earlier cell: 1.1 million from Wikipedia, then 1,503,263 which included 1944.
rows.source: GUS, Rocznik Statystyczny 1948, table 6 'Repatriacja z Z.S.R.R. do Polski', p. 28 (source: Państwowy Urząd Repatriacyjny), https://statlibr.stat.gov.pl/exlibris/aleph/a22_1/apache_media/SFGFA59FBIX2KUU9ER34EY9RMJ7TC8.pdf; 1948 from Henryk Bartoszewicz, Przegląd Historyczny 87(3), 1996, p. 572, https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/texts/przeglad-historyczny/1996-tom-87-numer-3/przeglad_historyczny-r1996-t87-n3-s563-578.pdf

Includes Polish Jews; excludes the 1944 arrivals and 1949.

rows.note: Individual returns from the USSR with Soviet passports and family reunification: about 1,600 in 1950-52 (MSZ), 1,096 in 1953 and 2,017 in 1954 (Biuletyn Informacyjny o Repatriacji); 4,713 in all. Two sources disagree on 1954: MSZ says about 400, which would give 3,096 for the period. Extras that may or may not be in these counts: 787 children by July 1952, 308 released from camps in 1951 (260 in March, 48 in September), a group of 358 under the amnesty on 9 Jan 1954. Later in the series: 6,429 by Oct 1955, which belongs to 1955-59. Cross-check: IPN gives 10,000 to 20,000 for all of 1948-55, and 7,325 (1948, Bartoszewicz) + 4,713 + 6,429 (1955 to Oct) is already 18,467 before 1949, so the three fit. No mass repatriation took place in these years; the borderland resettlement ended in 1946 and the Soviet side closed the question in the late 1940s.
rows.source: Ewelina Iwona Rytelewska, Prawne i polityczne aspekty przemieszczeń ludności polskiej z ZSRR, Studia Prawnoustrojowe 63, 2024, pp. 371-372 (citing AMSZ Zespół 7 via A. Paczkowski, Powrót żołnierzy AK z sowieckich łagrów, 1995, and the Biuletyn Informacyjny o Repatriacji), https://czasopisma.uwm.edu.pl/index.php/sp/article/download/9419/7379/35490
rows.method: Sum of persons who returned individually from the USSR: about 1,600 for 1950-52 (foreign ministry), 1,096 for 1953 and 2,017 for 1954 (repatriation bulletin). These two sources are joined here, and 1950-52 is one aggregate, not a year-by-year series.
rows.why: Two sources with different definitions are combined and disagree on 1954 (2,017 vs about 400); 1950-52 is a rounded sum; only individual returns are counted, with unclear overlap with children and camp releases.

rows.note: Poles (old settlers and their families, mostly from northern Bosnia around Banja Luka, a few from Croatia, Serbia and Slovenia) resettled to Poland under the Polish-Yugoslav protocol of 2 Jan 1946: 32 transports from 28 Mar to 5 Nov 1946, most of them settled in Bolesławiec County (Lower Silesia). The Mixed Commission's final protocol of 3 Nov 1946 gives 15,301 persons. Families: 2,930 (Baniecki, AP Wrocław) vs 3,924 (Oliwa); not resolved. PUR reports that include a 33rd transport (78 families, Banja Luka; the AP page says about 100 families in Sep 1947) and individual arrivals give about 20,000 by the end of 1948 (rounded; Oliwa also uses 'almost 20,000' for the county alone). About 2,000 Poles stayed in Yugoslavia. A search summary quoted 14,088 to 18,000 for Bosnia (Wikipedia, not used). Kamberović (Časopis za suvremenu povijest 30, 1998) has the Yugoslav side but its PDF could not be downloaded.
rows.source: Mieczysław Oliwa, Osadnictwo w powiecie bolesławieckim po II wojnie światowej, Studia z zakresu nauk prawnoustrojowych, Miscellanea 10, 2020, pp. 86-88 (citing AP Wrocław, PUR, sygn. 627, 1216), https://kpsw.edu.pl/pobierz/wydawnictwo/Miscellanea/T_%20X/Oliwa.pdf; Adam Baniecki, Osadnictwo Polaków z byłej Jugosławii w powiecie bolesławieckim 1946-1947 (AP Wrocław, PUR sygn. 794), https://www.wroclaw.ap.gov.pl/odcienie-regionalizmu/b_repzjug.html
rows.method: Persons moved to Poland from Yugoslavia in the organised 1946 resettlement, as confirmed by the Polish-Yugoslav Mixed Commission (3 Nov 1946) and quoted from the Wrocław archive files by two historians. Covers 1946 only.
rows.why: Lower bound read from secondary texts: the 1946 transports only, without the 1947 transport and individual arrivals (PUR total about 20,000 to end of 1948), and the two texts disagree on the number of families.

rows.note: Repatriates and reemigrants arriving from Czechoslovakia through the western PUR stations, July 1946 to December 1947: 1,536 (repatriates 1,201 + reemigrants 335); of these 872 in 1947 (551 + 321), so 664 in Jul-Dec 1946. The yearbook gives no country split for Jul-Dec 1945, Jan-Jun 1946 or 1948, when most of the movement through Czechoslovakia took place (the western stations received 656,182 people in Jul-Dec 1945 alone, mostly from Germany). A history blog quotes 14,502 arrivals from Czechoslovakia for 1945-47 at one station (Dziedzice) without naming a source; it was not verified and is not used, but it suggests that the true total is many times higher. Jiří Friedl's monograph on Poland's citizens in Czechoslovakia 1945-48 has the full numbers and was not available.

rows.method: Official PUR count of people who arrived from Czechoslovakia through the western stage stations (repatriates and reemigrants), July 1946 to December 1947 only (18 of the 60 months of the period).
rows.why: Covers only 18 months of the period and only the western stations; the large 1945 and early 1946 returns are not broken down by country, so this is a strong lower bound.

rows.note: Czechs and Slovaks who reemigrated from Poland to Czechoslovakia by the end of 1949, from the final report on the mass reemigration of Czechs and Slovaks from abroad (National Archive Prague, fond MPSP-R 1938-1951, carton 538). For comparison the same report gives, from other countries: USSR 42,580, Hungary 65,334, Romania 21,001, France 12,915, Austria 11,117, Yugoslavia 5,197, Germany 4,059. This is nationality-based (Czech or Slovak ethnicity) and counts to the end of 1949, so it covers the whole 1945-49 period, but includes people from the Czech enclaves in the Polish-held border areas and does not include the Poles' side of the exchange.
rows.source: Martin Nedvěd, Nemajetní krajané - plus pro stranu? Vliv KSČ na poválečnou reemigraci, Právněhistorické studie 53(2), 2023, pp. 147-158, footnote 30, quoting the archival report, https://karolinum.cz/data/clanek/11869/PHS_53_2_0147.pdf
rows.method: Number of Czech and Slovak reemigrants who moved from Poland to Czechoslovakia up to the end of 1949, as recorded in the Czechoslovak social welfare ministry's final report; ethnicity-based, cumulative from 1945.
rows.why: One archival figure read in a student paper, not in the report itself; it counts Czech and Slovak reemigrants only (not other people who moved to Czechoslovakia) and is a cumulative total to 1949 with no year split.

rows.note: Two non-overlapping windows added: 3,075 war refugees who left Romania for Poland from June 1945 to April 1946 (Nowak, citing Sowińska-Krupka 1985), and 4,208 people (371 repatriates + 3,837 reemigrants) who arrived from Romania through the western PUR stations between July 1946 and December 1947 (3,545 of them in 1947: 260 + 3,285; GUS Rocznik Statystyczny 1948, table 5B). The PUR figure fits Nowak's transports: 503 people in September 1946 and a further 3,403 by mid-July 1947 (770 of them war refugees and pre-war labour emigrants, the rest mostly from Southern Bukovina). Nowak also gives 4,858 former Romanian citizens who left in 1946-1950 in all (the last transport at the end of April 1950); the remainder for 1948-49 would be about 1,000 (4,858 minus 3,837 reemigrants) if the groups match, which was not verified and is not added. May-June 1946 is not covered by either window. A regional article's 45,000 Poles leaving 'Bukovina' in 1945-47 is not used: Bukovina was split between Romania and the Soviet Union, and that figure is not broken down.
rows.source: Krzysztof Nowak, Reemigracja polskich górników z Rumunii na Górny Śląsk po II wojnie światowej, Śląski Kwartalnik Historyczny Sobótka 73(4), 2018, pp. 77-102, https://www.repozytorium.uni.wroc.pl/Content/132960/PDF/04_K_Nowak_Reemigracja_polskich_gornikow_z_Rumunii.pdf; GUS, Rocznik Statystyczny 1948, table 5B (source: Państwowy Urząd Repatriacyjny), p. 28, https://statlibr.stat.gov.pl/exlibris/aleph/a22_1/apache_media/SFGFA59FBIX2KUU9ER34EY9RMJ7TC8.pdf
rows.method: Sum of two counts of people who left Romania for Poland: war refugees June 1945 to April 1946 (historian, from archival files) and repatriates plus reemigrants arriving through the western PUR stations July 1946 to December 1947 (official PUR table).
rows.why: Lower bound from two sources with different definitions: it leaves out May-June 1946 and 1948-49, and the first part is a single historian's figure; returns from Romania also passed through other routes than the western stations.

rows.note: Second repatriation, 1955-59: 245,000 'repatriated', of whom 22,000 came from labour camps and places of exile in the interior of the USSR and the rest from the former eastern borderlands (Dziurok, IPN). Ruchniewicz (2000, 1999 article) says almost a quarter of a million, about 100,000 from Belarus, 20,000 from inner Russia, Jews and non-Polish family members up to 8%, peak 1957-58, wave fading in the second half of 1959. Przystanek Historia (IPN) gives about 250,000; a search summary also quoted 220,000 for 1957-59 (Towpik, not opened). rows.source: Adam Dziurok, Społeczeństwo małej stabilizacji, IPN, https://ipn.gov.pl/pl/historia-z-ipn/archiwum/174154,Adam-Dziurok-Spoleczenstwo-malej-stabilizacji.pdf; Małgorzata Ruchniewicz, Tzw. repatriacja ludności polskiej z ZSRR w latach 1955-1959, Dzieje Najnowsze 31(2), 1999, https://rcin.org.pl//Content/45789/PDF/WA303_61724_A507-DN-R-31-2_Ruchniewicz.pdf
rows.method: Number of persons repatriated to Poland from the USSR under the 1955-59 repatriation, as reported by historians (year-by-year table not found); includes Jews and non-Polish family members.
rows.why: Rounded totals from historians' texts, not a published yearly table; sources differ by 5,000 to 30,000 depending on dates and definitions.

rows.method: Polish workers and their families who returned from France to Poland under the Franco-Polish reemigration agreements (convoys from May 1946 to December 1948), taken as the Polish count to the end of 1948.
rows.why: The counts conflict (51,000 French, 58,000 Polish, almost 70,000 in Sekowski, 78,000 to the end of 1950), France did not record every departure, and the figures cover the old labour emigration only, not the repatriation of displaced persons.
rows.note: Polish count to the end of 1948: about 58,000; the French count is about 51,000. Pawel Sekowski gives almost 70,000 for 1946-48, and the 1950 Polish census recorded 78,400 returnees from France (Dzieciuchowicz 2000), the same 78,000 by the end of 1950 (the last two years are doubted, because reemigration had stalled). Janine Ponty gives about 50,000 (French) and nearly 80,000 (Polish) and calls both contested. The French census counted 423,470 Poles in March 1946 and 269,269 in 1954, a fall that also reflects naturalisation and deaths.
rows.source: Grzegorz Pelczynski, 'Losy reemigrantow z Francji w okresie PRL i III RP', Studia Migracyjne - Przeglad Polonijny 2/2019 (https://ejournals.eu/pliki_artykulu_czasopisma/pelny_tekst/92bc8ed7-dabb-4bc7-8eb9-4e52a6ecc4a2/pobierz); Pawel Sekowski, Dzieje Najnowsze 2/2014 (http://rcin.org.pl/Content/47194/PDF/WA303_63632_A507-DN-R-46-2_Sekowski.pdf); Jerzy Dzieciuchowicz, 'Polonia francuska', Acta Universitatis Lodziensis, Folia Geographica Socio-Oeconomica 3/2000 (https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/texts/acta-universitatis-lodziensis-folia-geographica-socio-oeconomica/2000-numer-3/acta_universitatis_lodziensis_folia_geographica_socio_oeconomica-r2000-t-n3-s31-57.pdf); Janine Ponty, 'Les rapatriements d'ouvriers polonais (1945-1948)' (https://pbc.uw.edu.pl/24175/1/Ponty.pdf); INSEE 1999 census retrospective table R6 (https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/2118512)

rows.method: Estimated number of Poles who settled in Argentina in the postwar wave of 1946-50 (mostly soldiers of the Polish forces and their families, and displaced persons), taken as the lower end of a published range of 20,000 to 22,000.

rows.note: Stanislaw Pyzik puts the postwar settlers at 20,000-22,000; the Polish community priest cited by the Circulo Polones says about 16,000; a net-migration series gives 16,784 for 1941-50. Over 20,000 Polish citizens arrived but about 9,000 were registered as Poles.

rows.method: Estimated number of Poles who arrived in Brazil in the first postwar years, taken as the lower end of a published range of 10,000 to 20,000.
rows.why: No national count by nationality was found: estimates range from 10,000 to 30,000 for 1945-50, the only archive count (4,718 Poles, 1947-51) covers São Paulo's immigrant hostel records alone, and many displaced persons moved on to the United States and Canada.
rows.note: Wspolnota Polska gives 10,000-20,000 Poles in the first postwar years (1,481 displaced Poles from mid-1947 to mid-1948 and 7,397 by March 1950); another source gives about 30,000 for 1945-50. The Memorial do Imigrante records show 4,718 Poles entering São Paulo's hostel in 1947-51 (26% of 18,369 arrivals), 9% of whom later applied for exit visas, mostly for the United States.

rows.method: Polish soldiers of the 2nd Rifle Division interned in Switzerland since 1940 who went back to Poland when the internment ended in 1945 (the repatriation ran from 8 May to 15 December 1945).
rows.why: A round figure of about 2,000 that comes from one line in Polish secondary writing (it probably traces to Matyja's 2013 monograph, which I could not read). It covers soldiers only, not civilians, and excludes the many who moved on from France to Poland later.
rows.note: More than 12,000 men were interned (some sources say over 13,000). The claim that more than half of the division went home is contradicted by both the IPN article and dzieje.pl, which say most did not return.

rows.method: Greek and Macedonian children evacuated from the Greek Civil War to Poland: two rail transports in September-October 1948 (1,013) and groups in April 1949 (2,092).
rows.why: Only the children's transports are dated; the adult refugees are not counted here (the first adult group reached Zgorzelec on 16 December 1949), so this is a lower bound for 1945-49. Refugees, not migrants by choice, and not Greeks moving from Greece in a statistical sense.
rows.note: 1,013 + 2,092 = 3,105 children, from Nowicka. The IPN volume gives 'more than 3,000 children' evacuated, which agrees. Replaces an earlier 12,000 from Wikipedia that put all refugees in 1945-49.
rows.source: Ewa Nowicka, Forced Emigration and Desired Return: The Social and Psychological Consequences of the Wartime Evacuation of Greeks, Balcanica Posnaniensia XXIV (2017), https://pressto.amu.edu.pl/index.php/bp/article/view/6857

rows.method: Greek Civil War refugees (Greeks and Macedonians) who reached Poland from the end of 1949 and in the 1950s: the IPN total of 'more than 13,000' minus the 3,105 children counted under 1945-49.
rows.why: A lower bound derived by subtraction from one total whose period split is not published. It assumes the IPN total includes the children; the English summary says 'in addition more than 3,000 children', which would make the adult figure about 13,000. Some adults came with the children before 1950. Nowicka gives about 20,000 refugees in all, probably counting those born in Poland.
rows.note: Adults came from 16 December 1949 (Zgorzelec) and in 1950 (Nowicka). Other totals: 12,300 for 1948-51 and about 15,000 (secondary sources found by search, not read).
rows.source: Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), PRL a wojna domowa w Grecji / The Polish People's Republic and the Greek Civil War (ed. M. Semczyszyn, Szczecin 2016), publisher's summary, https://ipn.gov.pl/pl/wydawnictwo/do-pobrania/publikacje-obcojezyczne/233032,PRL-a-wojna-domowa-w-Grecji-The-Polish-Peoples-Republic-and-the-Greek-Civil-War.pdf

rows.method: Number of Polish citizens living in the United Arab Emirates according to the Polish embassy ('about 10 thousand'), entered as the people who moved there by 2024. It is a stock of residents, not a count of moves in 2020-24.
rows.why: The UAE publishes no migration flows by country and the UN table has no Poland-born stock for the UAE, so the only figure is an undated embassy estimate of Poles living there. It is rounded, not tied to a year, includes people who arrived before 2020, and misses Poles who have since left, so it is neither an upper nor a lower bound for 2020-24.
rows.note: Embassy text: the number of Polish citizens living in the UAE is 'rising intensively and is today about 10 thousand' (page mentions 2024 tourism figures, so it was written in 2025 or later). Wikipedia's article on Poland-UAE relations says 9,000 Poles live there as of 2024, citing The National (2025), which is consistent. Two lower figures (about 6,000 from a blog and about 3,000 from a 2013 market profile) appeared only in search summaries and the pages could not be opened, so they are not used. Earlier periods are empty because no dated earlier stock was found.
rows.source: Embassy of the Republic of Poland in Abu Dhabi, Bilateral relations, https://www.gov.pl/web/zea/relacje-dwustronne (read 2026-11-10)

rows.method: Number of Poles with resident status in the United Arab Emirates on 9 October 2013, as given by the Polish embassy in Abu Dhabi to Bankier.pl; entered as the people who had moved there by 2014. A stock of residents, not a count of moves in 2010-14.
rows.why: A stock of residents, not a count of moves in the period: it includes people who arrived earlier and misses those who left, and the UAE publishes no migration flows by country. The embassy figure counts residence-status holders only, so Poles registered elsewhere or on short visas are missed, and it is one reporter's request for one date.
rows.note: Bankier.pl, 9 October 2013: 2,348 Poles with resident status in the UAE, of whom 1,623 in Dubai (embassy data). An earlier search summary gave 2,016 for Dubai; the article says 1,623.
rows.source: Bankier.pl (M. Wrotniak), Polscy specjaliści w Dubaju: 40 tys. zł wypłaty nikogo nie dziwi, 2013-10-09, citing the Polish embassy in Abu Dhabi, https://www.bankier.pl/wiadomosc/Polscy-specjalisci-w-Dubaju-40-tys-zl-wyplaty-nikogo-nie-dziwi-2957608.html

rows.method: Number of Poles living in the United Arab Emirates 'according to various estimates' on the Polonia.org country page (page carries September 2019 dates); entered as the people who had moved there by 2019. A stock of residents, not a count of moves in 2015-19.
rows.why: A stock of residents, not a count of moves in the period: it includes people who arrived earlier and misses those who left, and the UAE publishes no migration flows by country. The page gives no method or exact year ('about 6 thousand', mostly people on contracts of a few years), so it is a rounded undated estimate.
rows.note: Polonia.org (Polacy w Zjednoczonych Emiratach Arabskich): about 6 thousand Poles, working in international companies, mostly on multi-year contracts, mainly in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, few staying permanently. Compare 2,348 residents in 2013 (embassy) and about 10,000 in the 2020-24 cell.
rows.source: Polonia.org, Polacy w Zjednoczonych Emiratach Arabskich, https://www.polonia.org/polacy-na-swiecie/polacy-w-zjednoczonych-emiratach-arabskich
